syllabus.clause: Fisher–Yates and the classic biased implementations

at.step: Fisher-Yates: for each position from the last down to the second, draw a position uniformly from everything not yet placed, and swap.
Swap each position with any position at all, not just the unplaced ones: that is far more choice chains than orderings, and the extra chains cannot divide evenly across them.

Sorting with a comparator that returns a random value is not a consistent ordering, so the result leans on the sorting algorithm’s own internals. A real browser-choice ballot shipped exactly this comparator.

A generator cannot produce more outcomes than it has internal states, however the shuffle uses its numbers — and taking a draw by remainder is biased whenever the generator’s own range does not split evenly by the size wanted.

Sattolo’s algorithm: the same loop, but the draw is strictly below the current position instead of at or below it. That one change forces a single cycle through every item, never the starting arrangement.

Write that same stricter draw where an ordinary shuffle was meant, and the bug hides in plain sight: the result is never the starting arrangement and never leaves anything in its own place, which a true shuffle would do once in a while.

syllabus.clause: shuffling data too large for memory

at.step: Three honest options once memory runs out: key every record and sort externally; split into buckets at random and shuffle each bucket in memory; or stream through a buffer, trading uniformity for a bounded window.

A buffer of a few slots, holding the stream and swapping a random slot each step: an item can leave only a little earlier than it arrived, but it can leave much later than it arrived, with shrinking odds the longer it waits.
